text: You built qresearch in the last lesson: a vectorized data and signal layer, one Numba hot path, a lookahead-safe backtest, a logged and reproducible run, a test suite, and a SQL-based secondary path. That's a working project. Whether it's a good project depends on what you do next — how you back up your performance claims, how you write it up, and how you talk about it. This lesson covers all three, and closes out the course.

A reviewer checking this repo looks for four specific things. Correctness tests pass, and you can show the run, not just claim it. Performance claims are backed by a real method — a stated baseline and enough trials to trust the number, not just "I used Numba so it's fast." The run is reproducible: clone it, run one command, get the same result. And the README is readable in two minutes, because if someone has to read every source file to understand the project, the README has failed at its one job.

Here's what a claim that survives scrutiny looks like. Time the naive version and the Numba version over several runs, not one lucky measurement, and report the baseline, the sample size, and the number of trials right next to the speedup number. "It's fast now" is a vibe. A stated method someone else can rerun is a claim.

When you present it, walk through the architecture top-down — data, computation, reporting — instead of narrating files in the order you wrote them. Lead with a design decision and the reason for it, not just the tool you used. Be upfront about what's out of scope; stating your limits reads as judgment, not as a gap. And be ready to run the tests and the benchmark live if asked — a project you can only describe is weaker than one you can demonstrate.

This course took you through six chapters that all land in this one library. Fast data handling with NumPy, pandas, Parquet, and Polars. Numerical computing and the profiling and compiled speedups that make the one hot path fast. Software engineering and research tooling — testing, packaging, logging, reproducible workflows. And database access for quants, SQL and columnar and time-series stores. The capstone is all six of those, in one small, correctly tested library.

That's Advanced Python for Quant Research. You've gone from "does it run" to "is it fast, correct, and reproducible enough that another engineer could pick it up" — that's the actual bar in this field. Next in the path is C++ for Quantitative Developers, where that same habit of profiling before optimizing carries into the language most low-latency trading systems are actually written in.
